codex.entry.core_workflow.title: The Core Workflow
codex.entry.core_workflow.content:
Forge Studio’s workflow is a loop: describe → generate → paint → iterate.

Type what you want to see in the prompt box, hit Generate, and the AI creates an image on your canvas. From there, you can paint on top of it, then generate again — the AI works with whatever is already on the canvas.

You’re building images with your hands and the AI together. Every generation can be a starting point, a refinement, or a complete reimagining.
codex.entry.core_workflow.deep: Studio auto-routes based on canvas state: blank canvas → txt2img, canvas with content → img2img, mask painted → inpainting. The function isCanvasBlank() is the sole source of truth for this routing — it checks actual pixel data, not a dirty flag. Denoise strength controls how much the AI changes existing content (1.0 = full replace, 0.3 = gentle refinement).
codex.entry.tutorials_and_tours.title: Interactive Tutorials & Tours
codex.entry.tutorials_and_tours.content:
Studio has interactive tutorials that walk you through features hands-on, in the actual UI. Three places to find them.

1. Show Me buttons in Codex. Many entries have a blue Show Me button at the top. Most open a new tab called “Tutorial: …” with a sample picture and walk you through the feature step by step. When you finish — or press End tour — the tutorial tab closes and you land back where you were, so your real work is never touched.

Available for: Setting Up Models, Basic Inpainting and Soft Inpainting, the Masks panel, Outpaint, the canvas right-click menu, Smart Patch, Paint Mixer, Develop local adjustments, Canvas Routing, Layers, Clone Stamp, Transform & Warp, Symmetry Painting, Brush Dynamics, the LoRA Browser and Wildcards. The Core Workflow and Making Your First Image replay the first-run walkthrough for your chosen path.

2. The first-run path picker. The first time you launched Studio, you saw a card with two options:

• I’m new to AI image generation — progressive walkthrough that makes your first image, then reveals controls in groups as you go. It branches to a model-setup step if Studio can’t see any models yet, and to an inpaint step if you click Result → Canvas. It persists — if you close mid-walkthrough, it resumes where you left off.

• I’ve used Stable Diffusion, Photoshop, or similar tools — spatial orientation tour. Full UI visible from the start, focuses on what’s different about Studio compared to other AI/art tools.

You can also skip and figure things out yourself.

3. Restart from Settings. Open the Settings tab at the top, then Appearance & Layout and the Accessibility card. Its Education section has two buttons:

• Restart Tour — replays your current path from the beginning.

• Change Path — brings the first-run picker back so you can switch between Beginner and Experienced.

The Workshop and Gallery tabs also show a short tour the first time you open them. None of these block you. You can dismiss any tour with Escape.
codex.entry.first_image.title: Making Your First Image
codex.entry.first_image.content:
1. Type a description in the prompt box — "a cat on a mountain at sunset" works fine.

2. Click Generate (or Ctrl+Enter).

3. Wait a few seconds. Your image appears in the output gallery.

4. Click Result → Canvas to place it on the canvas for editing.

Every image is unique — same prompt, different seed, different result. Try generating a few times to see the variety.

Nothing happens? Studio needs a model chosen first — see Models & VAE. The Jobs block under Generate says what is missing.
codex.entry.not_in_studio_yet.title: Not in Studio Yet
codex.entry.not_in_studio_yet.content:
Some things you may have seen in other tools — or in older versions of this one — are not available in Studio yet. Here is what to use instead.

ControlNet. Not available; there is no ControlNet panel. To keep a layout, paint or load a reference on the canvas and generate at a lower Denoise.

Live Painting. Not available. Paint, press Generate, repeat — the canvas is already the img2img input.

Regional Prompting. Not available. The Regions panel can still hold regions with your document, but they are not sent when you press Generate. For different content in different places, mask an area and regenerate it with its own prompt (see Masks Panel).

High Precision / float output. Not available. Export EXR converts the ordinary 8-bit picture, and Develop works on 8-bit pictures.

Batch Count and Batch Size. Removed. To make several images, submit several jobs — the queue runs them in order and lets you cancel or reorder any one (see Jobs & Queue).

Workshop: Test Merge and extra merge methods. Workshop has Weighted Sum, SLERP and Add Difference, block weights, LoRA and VAE baking, chains and History. Trying a merge in memory (Test Merge) and the other methods are not available.

Custom brush tips. The Custom brush preset is shown but disabled: Studio can’t load a tip image yet.

Inpaint Sketch mode. There isn’t one — paint on the canvas and use masks.

Extensions tab. It is a place for add-on panels; none are installed, so it is empty.
codex.entry.ui_layout.title: UI Layout
codex.entry.ui_layout.content:
Left: Toolstrip — your painting tools (brush, eraser, fill, and 16 more) plus the Inpaint Mask tool (Q).

Center: Canvas — scroll to zoom, Space+drag to pan. This is where your image lives. Right-click it for the canvas menu (Canvas Right-Click Menu).

Right: Panel — two tabs: Generate (prompt, LoRAs, Generate, model, sampling, Hires, Auto Detail, Upscale, layers and masks, history) and Extensions (add-on panels; none are installed, so it is empty). \ collapses the panel for more canvas space.

Top: Context bar — shows controls for whichever tool is active (size, opacity, hardness, etc.).

Bottom: Status bar — canvas dimensions, the model in use, and generation status.

Tab bar: Canvas, Develop, Gallery, Workshop, Wildcards, Codex (you’re here) and Settings — a page of its own with the model folders, save folder and everything else (see Settings Map).
codex.entry.models_and_vae.title: Models & VAE
codex.entry.models_and_vae.content:
The model (also called a checkpoint) is the AI brain that generates your images. Without one, Studio can’t generate anything. Different models produce completely different styles — photorealistic, anime, painterly, abstract.

Pointing Studio at your models:

1. Download a model file. Here’s a good one to start with: ToxicHost’s recommended starter model

2. Put it in a folder of its own.

3. Open Settings → General → Model folders. Add that folder as the Checkpoint folder — type the path or press Browse… (it opens your system’s own folder window) — then press Save folders.

4. Back on the Canvas, pick the model in the Model box. Added a file later? Press the refresh button (↻) beside it — no restart needed.

The same card has folders for text encoders, VAEs, Auto Detail detectors, LoRAs, embeddings and upscalers (the Hires and Upscale menus; Studio’s bundled upscaler stays listed). Studio lists only the files directly inside each folder, not subfolders, and skips shortcuts and links. A folder on another computer needs Allow network model folders switched on first; if that machine is off, the folder shows as Offline and Studio keeps working.

Choosing, loading, unloading: Picking a model, text encoder or VAE only records your choice. Generate loads what you chose — there is no Load button — so the first image after a change takes longer and later images reuse it. Settings → Performance & VRAM → Unload Model from VRAM frees the GPU.

Families: Studio works out a model’s family from the file. Checkpoints, LoRAs and detail models are not cross-compatible between families. Some families need more than a checkpoint — Anima, for example, uses a checkpoint plus a text encoder plus a VAE, so pick all three (see Anima).

Model formats:

• .safetensors — standard, always prefer this.

• .gguf — quantized, uses less VRAM at some quality cost. Good for larger models on smaller GPUs.

• fp16 / fp8 — numerical precision. Lower = less VRAM, slightly less quality. fp16 is the sweet spot for most.

VAE: The VAE handles color processing. Leave it on “Automatic” — most models include their own. If your colors look washed out or oversaturated, try switching to a specific VAE from the dropdown.

Find more models on CivitAI (checkpoints, LoRAs, community content) and Hugging Face (official releases).
codex.entry.models_and_vae.deep: Model folders are read on the machine running Studio; the refresh buttons rescan them. VAE “Automatic” uses the model’s baked-in VAE. For SD1.5 color issues try vae-ft-mse-840000. SDXL uses dual text encoders (CLIP-L + CLIP-G). Flux-style models need a separately downloaded text encoder.
codex.entry.output_workflow.title: Saving & Using Results
codex.entry.output_workflow.content:
Generated images appear in the output gallery strip at the bottom of the Generate panel.

Result → Canvas places the image on your canvas as a new layer — it doesn’t overwrite your existing work. Pipeline results (generation, upscale) go to a reusable "Gen Result" layer.

Save writes to disk using your default format and folder. Save As… downloads through your browser (you choose the name, place and format). The arrow beside them has more destinations: Save to Gallery and Export EXR (an EXR made from the ordinary 8-bit picture — there is no float capture).

Auto-save is Settings → Generation → Save outputs (on by default). The format and quality are under Settings → Output & Files → Output Format: PNG, JPEG or WebP. Embed metadata stores your prompt and settings inside saved files so other tools (PNG Info, other AI UIs) can read them later.

When auto-save is off: results may be written to temporary session scratch files for preview/history only — they are deleted when they fall out of the session history, on Clear session, and at server restart. Scratch is never written for saved outputs.

Where files go: Settings → Output & Files → Save folder. By default Studio saves under its results folder, in studio/<create|edit|upscaled>/<date>/. The Save tree choice can use Forge Neo’s own txt2img / img2img folders instead. To save somewhere else, type a path or press Browse…; a folder outside Studio’s trusted places falls back to the default and says so (Trust folder adds it).

File name: auto-saved files are named Studio-NNNNN-seed.ext — a 5-digit counter per folder and the exact seed — unless you set a pattern in Save folder → File name. Mix your own text with tokens such as [number] [seed] [date] [datetime] [model_name] [prompt_words] [steps] [cfg] [sampler] [width] [height] [mode]. For example [date]-[model_name]-[seed]. A preview line shows the result as you type. An unknown token or a path character is refused, the pattern names a file (never a folder), and an existing name is never overwritten. Leave it blank for the default.

Gallery always remembers: Studio’s Gallery tracks generation params for every image regardless of the Embed metadata setting. It uses a pixel fingerprint, so metadata survives file renames, moves between folders, and format conversions (PNG → JPG → WebP). Turning off Embed metadata only affects whether other tools can read it from the file itself.

Workflow defaults: Save your current parameter settings (sampler, scheduler, CFG, steps, denoise, and more) as defaults via Settings → General → Defaults → Save Current as Defaults. These persist server-side and load automatically on next launch. Separate from per-tool brush settings, which are client-side.
codex.entry.output_workflow.deep:
Gallery metadata is keyed by SHA256 of the decoded RGB pixel data, computed locally in compute_content_hash(). Generation writes the metadata row to the Gallery DB immediately via save_metadata_by_hash(), without waiting for a Gallery scan. When the scan later finds the file on disk, it links the existing hash-keyed metadata row to the filepath-keyed image row. Because the key is the pixel fingerprint, not the path, operations that preserve pixel identity (rename, move, lossless format conversion) keep the metadata attached. Lossy re-encoding will break the link — the new file has different pixels, so it gets a new hash.

The [number] counter is determined per folder at save time by scanning for existing Studio-NNNNN-* files and incrementing the highest match, so manual deletions in a folder don’t create gaps that get filled later. The pattern language follows Forge Neo’s file-name tokens for the values Studio has when it writes, plus [number] and [mode].
codex.entry.layouts.title: Layouts & Customize Mode
codex.entry.layouts.content:
Studio has two layout presets, switchable in Settings → Layout: Classic (the default — everything in the right panel) and Deck (prompt, LoRAs, negative, and Generate move to a deck row beneath the canvas, plus a vertical session strip between canvas and panel showing your recent results).

Customize mode: turn on Settings → Layout → Customize layout to rearrange the UI yourself. Panel sections become draggable blocks — drag them to reorder the panel, or (under Deck) drop them into the deck row. Most blocks show a small ✕ to hide them; hidden blocks collect in a tray at the bottom of the panel, where one click restores them. The prompt and Generate blocks can’t be hidden. While customizing you can also drag the panel’s left edge to resize it (420–900 px). Customize mode needs a window at least 1600 px wide and is unavailable while generating — starting a generation exits it cleanly.

Saving & sharing layouts: layouts are saved server-side as named JSON files via Settings → Layout (Save, Save as…, Load, Delete). The files live in Studio’s own studio_layouts/ folder and ARE the export format — drop a shared layout JSON into studio_layouts/ and it appears in the Load list. Loading is resilient: block ids the file mentions but your install doesn’t have are dropped, and blocks the file doesn’t mention appear in their factory position.

Session strip: the Deck strip mirrors your session history (newest first). Click to select, double-click to open in Gallery, ‹ to collapse it to a slim rail. Its collapsed/hidden state is part of the layout.

Privacy note: with Save outputs off, results may be written to temporary session scratch files for preview/history only — deleted when they fall out of the session history, on Clear session, and at server restart. Scratch is never written for saved outputs.
codex.entry.layouts.deep: Layout state is a small JSON map (schema, base, zones, hidden, panelWidth, strip). Blocks are existing DOM sections registered with hidden position markers; applying a layout MOVES the original elements (never clones), so IDs, listeners, and control state survive every re-mount. The factory layouts restore byte-identical DOM. Layout files are validated server-side: slug-only names, 64 KB cap, typed shape checks, atomic writes.
codex.entry.color_picker.title: Color Picker
codex.entry.color_picker.content:
Click the toolstrip swatches to open the color picker. HSV wheel + hex input for precise colors.

X swaps foreground and background colors. D resets them to black and white.

Ctrl+Click on the canvas samples a color from any tool without switching away. I switches to the dedicated eyedropper tool.

Studio keeps a rolling history of your last 10 colors as clickable swatches below the picker.
codex.entry.canvas_routing.title: Canvas Routing
codex.entry.canvas_routing.content:
Studio doesn’t have separate txt2img and img2img tabs. You paint on the canvas, hit Generate, and Studio checks the pixels to decide the routing:

• Canvas is blank → txt2img (generates from scratch)

• Canvas has content → img2img (works with what’s there)

• Mask selected → inpainting (changes only the masked area — the Inpaint mask, or any named mask selected in the Masks panel)

You never pick a mode. The canvas state is the mode. If you sketch something, erase it all, and generate — that’s txt2img, because the canvas is blank. The pixels are the source of truth, not a mode toggle.

Zoom behavior: At 200%+ zoom, pixels render crisp (nearest-neighbor) instead of blurry. Below 200%, standard bilinear smoothing applies. This matches Krita’s behavior and makes pixel-level editing clean.
codex.entry.canvas_routing.deep: isCanvasBlank() checks actual pixel data on every generation call. It’s the sole source of truth for routing — no dirty flags or mode toggles involved. A completely transparent canvas routes to txt2img. Any non-transparent pixel routes to img2img. Mask presence is checked separately and takes priority.
codex.entry.documents.title: Documents & Tabs
codex.entry.documents.content:
Studio is a multi-document editor. The thin tab strip across the top of the canvas area lets you keep several separate workspaces open at once, like tabs in a browser or Photoshop.

Each document is fully independent. When you switch tabs, Studio swaps the entire workspace:

• Layers, mask, selection, and regional prompt boxes

• Undo/redo stack

• Zoom level and pan position

• The entire Generate panel — prompt, negative, seed, sampler, CFG, steps, denoise, dimensions, batch, HiRes Fix settings, all 3 ADetailer slots, Soft Inpainting, inpaint area/fill/blur/padding

So Doc 1 can be a portrait you’re refining at 768×1024 with one prompt and seed, while Doc 2 is a landscape experiment at 1216×832 with a completely different prompt. Switching between them is instant — nothing bleeds across.

Working with tabs:

• + button at the end of the strip — creates a new blank document.

• Click a tab to switch to it.

• × on hover — closes that document. You can’t close the last one. Closing a document with unsaved canvas changes prompts for confirmation.

• Right-click a tab for Close, Close other tabs and Close all tabs; right-click the empty strip for Close all tabs alone. Closing every tab leaves one fresh blank document. If any of the tabs being closed have unsaved changes, Studio asks once and says how many.

• Double-click a tab name to rename inline. Enter to commit, Escape to cancel.

• Ctrl+] and Ctrl+[ cycle forward and backward through documents.

• A small dot (•) appears next to a tab’s name when it has unsaved changes since the last snapshot.

Show Me tutorials use this system. When you click a Show Me button in Codex, Studio opens the tutorial in a new document so your real work stays untouched. When the tutorial ends (or you press End tour), the tutorial tab closes by itself.
codex.entry.documents.deep: Implemented in studio-docs.js. Each document holds a full snapshot: layers[], activeLayerIdx, mask, regions, undoStack/redoStack, zoom, panX/panY, W/H, plus the Generate panel state (values, selects, textareas, checkboxes — see _GEN_VALUES/_GEN_SELECTS/_GEN_TEXTAREAS/_GEN_CHECKS in the source). _saveDoc() snapshots to the current index; _loadDoc() restores a target. Switching always saves the outgoing doc first so no work is lost. Uses a multi-page pattern — the live canvas state is a window into the active document, not a separate store.
codex.entry.crash_recovery.title: Crash Recovery
codex.entry.crash_recovery.content:
Your work survives a refresh. If you press F5, the browser tab crashes, or you restart Studio, the canvas documents you had open come back: layers, masks, selection and zoom.

What does not come back: the undo history. A recovered document starts with an empty undo history — the pixels return, the ability to step back past the crash does not.

Closing a tab discards its recovery. Closing a document is the one thing that removes it; an ordinary export or save is not a project save and leaves recovery alone.

A refresh is not a backup: keep separate copies of artwork you care about, and report any document that did not come back.
codex.entry.scrub_labels.title: Scrub Labels
codex.entry.scrub_labels.content:
The context bar values (Size, Opacity, Hardness, Smoothing, Strength) aren’t traditional sliders — they’re scrub labels:

• Drag horizontally on the label to adjust the value (like Photoshop’s scrubby sliders).

• Click the label to open a text input and type an exact number.

Sensitivity scales to the value range — fine controls (like hardness 0–1) scrub slower than coarse ones (like size 1–100). You’ll get used to these fast.
codex.entry.per_tool_memory.title: Per-Tool Settings Memory
codex.entry.per_tool_memory.content:
Each brush-type tool (brush, eraser, smudge, blur, dodge, clone, liquify, shape) remembers its own settings independently. Size, opacity, hardness, smoothing, and strength are stored per-tool.

Switch from brush to eraser and back — your brush settings are exactly where you left them. These persist across sessions via local storage.
codex.entry.shift_drag_resize.title: Shift+Drag Brush Resize
codex.entry.shift_drag_resize.content:
Hold Shift and drag on the canvas: horizontal movement adjusts brush size, vertical movement adjusts opacity. Krita-style.

Works for brush, eraser, smudge, blur, dodge, clone, and liquify. Much faster than reaching for the context bar or using bracket keys.
codex.entry.drag_and_drop.title: Drag & Drop
codex.entry.drag_and_drop.content:
Drop an image file onto the canvas and Studio:

1. Resizes the canvas to match the image dimensions.

2. Creates a new layer with the image.

3. Updates width/height inputs and AR indicator.

4. Reads PNG metadata and imports generation parameters if found (prompt, seed, settings).

5. Disables Hires Fix automatically (since you’re loading an existing image).

This is the fastest way to bring an external image into Studio for editing or img2img.
codex.entry.send_to_canvas.title: Send to Canvas
codex.entry.send_to_canvas.content:
Sending an output to the canvas (button, right-click, or drag from the output strip) creates a new layer — it doesn’t overwrite your work.

Pipeline results (generation, upscale) go to a reusable "Gen Result" layer. Gallery sends also create new layers. Your painted edits on other layers are always safe.
codex.entry.ar_buttons.title: Aspect Ratio Buttons
codex.entry.ar_buttons.content:
The AR buttons have interactive behavior beyond simple presets:

• Click a ratio → applies it and resizes the canvas.

• Re-click the active ratio → swaps portrait/landscape (e.g. 3:2 becomes 2:3).

• Both actions are undoable — Ctrl+Z restores the previous canvas and dimensions.

When AR Randomization is enabled, the buttons switch to pool-toggle mode — click to include/exclude ratios from the random pool instead of applying them directly. Same behavior for base resolution buttons.
codex.entry.wildcards_editor.title: The Wildcards Tab
codex.entry.wildcards_editor.content:
The Wildcards tab in the main tab bar is an editor for your wildcard files. The Wildcards entry under Generation covers what wildcards are and the __name__ syntax — this entry is about the editor itself.

Which folder: the tab edits the wildcard folder you chose in Settings → Prompts & Metadata → Dynamic Prompts → Wildcard folder. With none chosen it says “No wildcard folder is chosen”.

Layout: File tree on the left, editor on the right. Click any file in the tree to open it. The dot next to the filename turns amber when there are unsaved changes.

Creating files and folders: Use + File and + Folder at the top of the tree. New files open immediately for editing. Folders nest — a file at characters/hair.txt is referenced as __characters/hair__ in your prompts.

Right-click a file or folder for rename, duplicate, move, and delete. You can also drag files between folders directly in the tree.

Search: the search box filters the tree by filename.

Live preview: Open the preview pane to see resolved sample lines from your wildcard file — including nested wildcards if your file references other wildcards. Refreshes as you edit.

Sort and duplicates: Sort reorders a file’s lines (click again to cycle the order); Remove duplicate entries drops repeated lines.

Auto-save: Toggle on to save changes ~1.5 seconds after you stop typing. Off by default — use Ctrl+S or the Save button manually if you prefer.
codex.entry.session_vs_defaults.title: Session Memory vs Workflow Defaults
codex.entry.session_vs_defaults.content:
Studio has two separate ways to make your settings persist between launches. They overlap in confusing ways, so here’s the difference.

Workflow Defaults — a saved baseline you set deliberately. Settings → General → Defaults → Save Current as Defaults snapshots your current parameters (sampler, CFG, steps, dimensions, AD slots, etc.) and saves them server-side. Every launch starts from this baseline. Use Reset to clear them and go back to factory settings.

Think of this as: "this is how I want Studio to start every time."

Remember Last Session — picks up where you left off. Toggle on in Settings → General → Session. Your prompts and settings save automatically when you close the page and restore on the next launch. Stored in your browser, not on the server.

Think of this as: "don’t make me retype my prompt every time I refresh."

Picking which categories Session Memory saves: When the toggle is on, an accordion appears with checkboxes for each category. Uncheck what you don’t want carried over.

• Prompts — positive and negative prompt text.

• Generation params & AR pools — sampler, scheduler, CFG, steps, dimensions, AR randomization pools.

• Hires Fix — enabled state, upscaler, scale, denoise, etc.

• ADetailer — all 3 slots’ enable state, model, prompts, confidence, denoise.

• Upscale — upscaler model, scale, post-AD toggle.

• Canvas settings — grid, pen pressure, save outputs, live preview, metadata, panel collapse states.

• Brush settings — brush size.

• Output format — PNG/JPEG/WebP and quality.

• Inpaint settings — area mode, fill, mask blur, padding.

Which order they apply: If both are active on launch, Session Memory wins — it loads last, on top of Defaults. Categories you unchecked in Session fall back to whatever Defaults have.

Quick guide:

• Want to always start with the same baseline? Defaults.

• Want continuity between sessions? Session Memory.

• Want both? Set Defaults to your ideal baseline, turn Session Memory on, uncheck the categories you want Defaults to win for.

Session Memory feature suggested by Railer.
codex.entry.settings_map.title: Settings Map
codex.entry.settings_map.content:
Settings is the tab at the top right. Its list on the left has ten groups:

• General — Model folders (where Studio looks for checkpoints, text encoders, VAEs, detectors, LoRAs, embeddings and upscalers), Session (Remember last session, history size, Clear session) and Defaults (Save Current as Defaults).

• Appearance & Layout — language, theme, Layout (Classic or Deck, Customize), Saved Layouts, and Accessibility, which holds the Education buttons (Restart Tour, Change Path).

• Canvas & Tools — grid, GPU canvas preview, how hard mouse strokes press.

• Generation & Preview — Save outputs, Always show all parameters, Live preview and its quality.

• Prompts & Metadata — tag suggestions, Tidy prompt on generate, dynamic prompts and the wildcard folder, and Civitai lookup.

• Output & Files — Output Format, Save to Gallery, Save folder (folder, Save tree, File name), Heatmap data and Watermark.

• Performance & VRAM — GPU, GPU Weights, Unload Model, Auto-unload, GPU tile compositing (see VRAM & Performance).

• Keyboard Shortcuts — every shortcut can be remapped; Reset all to defaults undoes it.

• Extensions — an on/off list of add-on panels (none are installed today).

• About — version, Check for Updates (Git installations) and credits.

Browse… Every folder setting (model folders, Save folder, Gallery folder, wildcards, heatmap data) has a Browse… button that opens your system’s own folder window (Windows’ “Select Folder”, or Finder on a Mac). Typing a path still works.

Going online: Studio only goes online when you press a button that says so — Civitai lookup in the model browsers, and Check for Updates. Nothing updates automatically.
codex.entry.workflows.title: Workflows
codex.entry.workflows.content:
A workflow is a named set of generation settings you can re-apply later — a model with its sampler, steps, CFG and size, for example. The row below the Generate button has the controls:

• Save — save the current settings as a new workflow. You name it, add a description and a model family, and choose whether it includes the prompt, the negative prompt and the dimensions.

• Apply — apply the selected workflow to this tab. If its dimensions differ from the canvas you choose between applying the settings only or resizing the canvas too.

• New Tab — open the selected workflow in a new tab, leaving your current one alone.

• Delete — remove the selected workflow.

Applying a workflow does not load its model at once; the model loads on your next Generate. If a saved setting is not available any more, the workflow applies the rest and tells you how many were skipped.

Workflows are different from Workflow defaults (the baseline Studio starts from every launch) — see Session Memory vs Workflow Defaults.
codex.entry.tool_brush.title: Brush
codex.entry.tool_brush.content:
Your primary painting tool. Adjust Size, Opacity, Hardness and Density in the context bar. Hardness controls edge softness — 100% is a sharp circle, lower values give a softer, airbrushed look. Smoothing stabilizes your strokes for cleaner curves. [/] to resize quickly.

Four presets, each suited to different tasks:

• Round — general purpose, clean edges. Your default for most painting.

• Flat — wide strokes with angle sensitivity. Good for broad fills and gradients.

• Scatter — textured spray of particles. Use for foliage, gravel, stars, or organic noise.

• Marker — firm edge with slight texture. Good for linework and outlines.

The Custom button is shown but disabled: Studio can’t load a brush-tip image yet.

Also in the bar: Alias (hard pixel edges, no antialiasing) and PP (pixel-perfect one-pixel corners; needs Alias and a 1 px brush); Mix, which picks up and carries wet colour (see Paint Mixer); the symmetry buttons (see Symmetry Painting); and Pen pressure.

Pressure sensitivity: The Pen button turns pen pressure on; the S (pressure → size) and O (pressure → opacity) buttons beside it choose what it drives. The Brush Dynamics panel (gear icon) exposes Follow stroke, Buildup, spacing, size/opacity/rotation jitter, scatter, the brush shape (ratio, density, spikes, angle, taper, falloff) and the document’s Paper texture.
codex.entry.tool_brush.deep: The opacity model uses a wet buffer — stamps draw at full opacity into a per-stroke buffer, and the completed stroke composites at the opacity ceiling. This prevents accumulation artifacts within a single stroke, matching Photoshop’s behavior. Brush dynamics include: spacing (fraction of diameter between stamps), size jitter, opacity jitter, scatter (random offset), rotation jitter, and follow-stroke rotation. Elliptical ratio and stipple/spike tips use Gaussian falloff via erf().
codex.entry.tool_eraser.title: Eraser
codex.entry.tool_eraser.content: Removes paint, making pixels transparent. On the background/reference layer, fills with white instead. Same controls and presets as the brush — size, opacity, hardness, dynamics all work the same way.
codex.entry.tool_eyedropper.title: Eyedropper
codex.entry.tool_eyedropper.content:
Click to sample a color from the canvas. Shortcut: Ctrl+Click from any brush tool samples without switching away.

Supports configurable radius averaging — instead of picking a single pixel, it averages an area around the sample point. Useful for getting a representative color from textured or noisy AI-generated regions.
codex.entry.tools_touchup.title: Touch-Up Tools
codex.entry.tools_touchup.content:
Four brush-style tools for refining what’s already on the canvas. They all share the brush’s size and hardness controls; each adds its own Strength slider to control how aggressively it applies per stroke.

Smudge S — blends colors like wet paint. Drag to pull color in the direction of your stroke. Best for softening AI-generated edges that look too sharp — skin boundaries, hair edges, clothing folds. Strength around 30–50% gives the most controllable results.

Blur R — paints softness in place. Good for smoothing skin, softening backgrounds, or reducing noise in specific areas without affecting the whole image. Unlike Smudge, it doesn’t move pixels — it only blurs them where you paint. Switch the bar from Blur to Sharpen to crisp up the pixels under the brush instead — good for rescuing soft eyes or text.

Dodge / Burn J — Dodge lightens, Burn darkens. Toggle between them in the context bar. Adjusts lighting without changing the underlying colors — great for adding depth, shadows, highlights, or correcting uneven lighting in generated images.

Pixelate P — paints a pixelated/mosaic effect into the brushed area. Pixel block size scales with brush size; Strength controls how strong the pixelation is per stroke (lower values blend partially with the original). Useful for censoring faces, license plates, or text in generated images, or for stylized 8-bit aesthetic edits.

All four tools work with selections — if a selection is active, edits are constrained to it. They also remember their settings independently per tool (see Per-Tool Settings Memory).
codex.entry.tool_clone.title: Clone Stamp
codex.entry.tool_clone.content:
Copies pixels from one part of the canvas to another. Here’s how to use it:

1. Hold Alt and click on a clean area near the thing you want to remove. This sets the source point.

2. Now paint over the unwanted object. The tool copies pixels from the source area as you paint, covering the object with matching content.

3. The source point follows your brush — it moves relative to where you paint. If the clone starts picking up wrong content, Alt+click a new source.

Works great for removing watermarks, erasing unwanted objects, duplicating elements, or patching artifacts in generated images.

The bar above the canvas has three modes: Clone (copies exactly), Heal (copies the source’s detail but keeps the colour and light of the spot you paint) and Patch (needs no source). See Smart Patch, Heal & Patch.
codex.entry.tool_liquify.title: Liquify
codex.entry.tool_liquify.content:
Pushes and warps pixels. Drag to distort the image in the direction you move. Great for adjusting proportions and fixing AI anatomy issues.

Use a large brush for broad adjustments (shoulder width, head tilt), small brush for fine-tuning (eye positions, jawlines, hand proportions). The distortion applies on stroke end.
codex.entry.tools_drawing.title: Fill, Gradient, Shape & Text
codex.entry.tools_drawing.content:
Fill G — flood-fills an area with the foreground color. Tolerance sets how different a pixel can be and still be filled, Contiguous (on by default) fills only the connected area — turn it off to fill every matching pixel on the layer — and Opacity is the fill’s real opacity.

Gradient G again — draws a smooth transition from foreground to background color. Linear or radial.

Shape U — rectangle, ellipse, or line. Fill or outline mode. Hold Shift for perfect squares/circles.

Text T — click to place, choose font and size. Renders to pixels on commit.
codex.entry.tools_selection.title: Selection Tools
codex.entry.tools_selection.content:
Create selections to constrain painting, generation, or clipboard operations to a specific area.

• M Rectangular — click and drag a box.

• O Elliptical — click and drag an oval. Shift constrains to circle.

• L Lasso — freehand selection. Three modes via context bar subtool buttons: freehand lasso, polygon lasso (click-to-click straight segments), and magnetic lasso (snaps to edges).

• W Magic Wand — selects similar-colored areas. Strength controls tolerance.

Ctrl+D deselect • Ctrl+A select all • Ctrl+Shift+I invert • Ctrl+C/X/V clipboard • Delete clear selection.

Every selection tool follows the same rules: each change is an undo step, and a document’s selection is kept when you switch tabs and after a reload. Right-click for Feather, Grow and Shrink Selection and for Smart Patch (see Canvas Right-Click Menu).
codex.entry.tools_selection.deep: The magnetic lasso uses Sobel edge detection combined with Dijkstra’s shortest-path algorithm to find the strongest edge path between anchor points. It snaps to high-contrast boundaries in the image, making it much faster than freehand for complex organic shapes.
codex.entry.tool_crop.title: Crop
codex.entry.tool_crop.content:
Trims the canvas to a selected region. Drag the crop box, then press Enter to apply or Escape to cancel.

The context bar offers AR-matching presets — common aspect ratios that snap the crop box to exact proportions. Useful for preparing images for specific output sizes.

To grow or trim the canvas without cropping, or to extend it for Outpaint, use the right-click menu — see Outpaint & Canvas Size.
codex.entry.tool_transform.title: Transform
codex.entry.tool_transform.content:
Move, scale, and rotate the current layer or selection. Drag handles to resize, drag inside to move. Enter applies, Escape cancels, Shift constrains proportions. The X, Y, W, H and R° boxes in the bar take exact numbers; Flip H/V and the rotate buttons (90°, 180°, any angle) do the common cases in one click. Transform also moves an ellipse or lasso selection’s shape, not just its box.

Modes (buttons in the bar while Transform is active):

• Skew (K) — edge handles shear the shape.

• Persp (P) — perspective: drag the four corners freely for correction or deliberate distortion.

• Warp (W) — free deformation: place control points and drag them. Then choose how it deforms: Aff (affine — most flexible), Sim (similitude — preserves angles; scale and rotate only) or Rig (rigid — preserves distances as much as possible, best for repositioning elements naturally). A grid-density choice (3, 4, …) sets the quality.

A toggles the aspect lock; H and V flip while a transform is active.

All warp modes use Moving Least Squares (MLS) interpolation for smooth, natural-looking deformations.
codex.entry.tool_transform.deep: The MLS warp implementation follows the Schaefer, McPhail & Warren paper with three deformation types (Affine, Similitude, Rigid). Grid subdivision renders the warp by tessellating the canvas into a grid and transforming each cell, avoiding the visual artifacts that per-pixel sampling would produce. The perspective transform uses standard 4-point homography. Algorithms ported from Krita’s GPL-3.0 source (tool_transform2/), which is license-compatible with Studio’s AGPL-3.0 via Section 13.
codex.entry.tool_radial_symmetry.title: Symmetry Painting
codex.entry.tool_radial_symmetry.content:
Studio supports three symmetry modes, toggled from the context bar buttons:

• Horizontal — mirrors strokes left/right across a vertical center line.

• Vertical — mirrors strokes top/bottom across a horizontal center line.

• Radial — replicates strokes around a center point with configurable axis count. Set 2 for simple mirror, 6+ for snowflake/kaleidoscope patterns, 8+ for mandala designs.

Works with brush, eraser, and smudge. In radial mode, each symmetry segment maintains its own independent smudge buffer so smudge strokes don’t bleed between segments.

Combined mode (horizontal + vertical) gives four-way symmetry.
codex.entry.canvas_menu.title: Canvas Right-Click Menu
codex.entry.canvas_menu.content:
Right-click anywhere on the canvas. Some items only show when they apply:

Selection — Select All, Deselect, and (with a selection active) Invert Selection, Feather…, Grow… and Shrink Selection…, plus Smart Patch, which fills the selection from the picture around it with no model.

Clipboard — Copy, Cut, Paste, Delete.

Layers — New Layer, Duplicate Layer, Merge Down, Flatten Visible.

Canvas — Canvas Size… and Outpaint… (see Outpaint & Canvas Size). These two have no other entry point. Zoom to Fit.

Output — Open in New Tab opens the flattened picture as a PNG in a new browser tab (allow pop-ups for Studio if your browser blocks it). Save as PNG, JPEG or WebP downloads the flattened picture; Save as PSD (layers) keeps the layers.
codex.entry.tool_smart_patch.title: Smart Patch, Heal & Patch
codex.entry.tool_smart_patch.content:
Ways to remove or hide small things without a model:

Patch — pick the Clone tool (K) and choose Patch in the bar. Paint over the blemish; when you let go it is filled from the picture around it. No source point needed.

Smart Patch from a selection — select the area with any selection tool, right-click inside it and choose Smart Patch. It works on a layer, not on a mask.

Heal — also in the Clone bar. Like Clone (Alt-click sets the source), but it copies the source’s detail while keeping the colour and light of the spot you paint, so the patch blends in.

Sharpen — in the Blur tool (R), switch from Blur to Sharpen to crisp up the pixels under the brush.

These work best on small things against a plain-ish background. For anything large, mask it and use inpainting.
codex.entry.tool_paint_mixer.title: Paint Mixer
codex.entry.tool_paint_mixer.content:
The brush can mix colour like wet paint. Turn on Mix in the bar when the Brush is selected: the brush picks up the colour under it and carries it along the stroke, and colours mix as pigment, so blue and yellow make green rather than a flat yellow on top.

Amount sets how much of the picked-up colour the brush carries: 0 is the plain brush colour, 100 only what it picked up. The brush recharges with fresh paint so a stroke still covers what is under it.

Turn Mix off to go back to ordinary painting.
codex.entry.param_prompt.title: Writing Effective Prompts
codex.entry.param_prompt.content:
Describe what you want to see in plain language. "A red fox in a snowy forest" works. So does "portrait of a woman with gold earrings, oil painting style, cinematic lighting." More specific prompts give more controlled results.

Structure: A good pattern is subject first, then style, then quality. For example: "a knight standing on a cliff overlooking a valley, fantasy art, dramatic lighting, highly detailed." The AI pays the most attention to words near the beginning, so front-load what matters most.

Emphasis: Control word strength with parentheses:

(important word:1.3) — 30% stronger. (less important:0.7) — 30% weaker. Plain (word) defaults to 1.1. Nesting stacks: ((word)) = 1.21. Stay in the 0.5–1.5 range — extreme values cause artifacts. Use sparingly; overweighting everything defeats the purpose.

BREAK: Forces a chunk boundary between sections. Useful for separating concepts that interfere with each other. A structured approach:

style, lighting, composition BREAK subject count BREAK detailed description, pose, background

Establishing "how it looks" before "what it is" helps consistent stylistic choices. Simple prompts don’t need BREAK — it shines with complex, detailed generations.

Token counter: The counter below the prompt shows token usage. The AI processes text in ~75-token chunks. Going past one chunk is fine, but words in later chunks may have less influence.

Patterns that work well:

• Quality tags: "masterpiece, best quality, highly detailed"

• Lighting: "soft natural light," "dramatic rim lighting," "golden hour"

• Camera: "close-up portrait," "wide shot," "low angle," "85mm lens"

• Art styles: "watercolor," "oil painting," "anime style," "digital painting"

• Specificity over vagueness: "burgundy velvet dress" beats "nice dress"

Prompt troubleshooting:

• Wrong number of subjects: Reinforce with solo. Move count tags earlier. Add multiple girls to negatives.

• Style not coming through: Front-load style tags. Use multiple related descriptors.

• Background overwhelming subject: Add blurred background, bokeh, depth of field. Move subject earlier.

• Concepts bleeding together: Add more BREAKs. Try prompt scheduling for staged introduction.
codex.entry.param_prompt.deep:
Advanced syntax:

Prompt Scheduling [from:to:when] — transitions between concepts during generation. when is a decimal (fraction of steps) or integer (exact step). Example: [sketch:finished rendering:0.5] starts sketch-like, transitions to polished at 50%. Shorthand: [to:when] adds "to" after a step; [from::when] removes "from" after a step. Does NOT work with LoRA or Hypernetworks.

Prompt Alternating [concept|concept] — alternates each step, creating blended effects. [red hair|blonde hair] produces strawberry blonde. [rain|snow] creates mixed precipitation. Does NOT work with LoRA or Hypernetworks.

Composable Diffusion AND — processes prompts separately and combines results. a portrait of a woman AND cyberpunk style. Supports per-section weights: a cat :1.2 AND a dog AND a penguin :2.2. Commas = single combined concept; AND = separate processing then merge. Can cause "overbaked" results at high CFG — lower to ~5.

Escaping — literal brackets with backslash: anime_\(character\). Comments after # are ignored by some extensions.

Extra Networks — <lora:filename:multiplier> and <hypernet:filename:multiplier> are processed and removed from the prompt before generation. Cannot be used in negative prompts or with scheduling/alternating.

Token counter shows per-encoder counts (CLIP-L and CLIP-G for SDXL) and chunk count. Multiple chunks work via prompt chunk concatenation — later chunks have full attention within themselves but reduced cross-chunk influence. Wildcard syntax __wildcard_name__ resolved before encoding via dynamicprompts.

On Anima (Studio weights, the default): the whole prompt is read as one piece, so brackets alone never change the picture. A weight changes how strongly a word attends: (word:1.6) often brings a missing object in while keeping the picture, and 2.0 often reshapes it. (word:0) silences the word but cannot remove what the rest of the prompt implies (“white dress” still draws a woman) — use the negative prompt or delete the word. BREAK has no effect on Anima: there are no 75-token chunks to separate. Reusing a weighted image made elsewhere switches to Neo-compatible weights, so it reproduces exactly.
codex.entry.anima.title: Anima
codex.entry.anima.content:
Anima is one of the model families Studio generates with. It uses a checkpoint, a text encoder and a VAE together — choose all three in the Model block (see Models & VAE).

Prompts: Anima reads the whole prompt as one piece, so there are no 75-token chunks and BREAK has no effect. Brackets alone don’t change the picture; a weight like (word:1.6) does. By default Studio uses its own Studio weights for Anima. A picture whose settings were made elsewhere (or before this was added) switches to Neo-compatible weights so it reproduces exactly.

Hires: Anima’s Hires pass runs at the same shift as its base pass (as Forge Neo does).

Heatmaps: Anima and SDXL pictures can record where each prompt word landed, which powers Word Heatmaps, word masks and Word Detail.
codex.entry.jobs_queue.title: Jobs & Queue
codex.entry.jobs_queue.content:
The Jobs block in the Generate panel shows what is running, what is waiting and what finished.

Press Generate while a job is running and the new job joins the queue. You can cancel or reorder any waiting job, and Clear queued drops them all. Interrupt stops the running job at its next safe point — not necessarily at once. This replaces Batch Count and Batch Size: to make several images, submit several jobs.

If Generate is refused, the block says why — for example “Select an available Studio model.”

Unload model in the same block releases the model from VRAM.
codex.entry.param_neg.title: Negative Prompt
codex.entry.param_neg.content:
Tells the AI what to avoid. Common negatives: "blurry, ugly, deformed, extra fingers, bad anatomy, watermark, text."

A few key words is usually enough — long negative prompts have diminishing returns. Only negate things you genuinely don’t want. If you say "red" in positive and "red" in negative, they fight each other and you get muddy results.

Wildcards like __neg4__ can insert pre-made negative templates if you have wildcard files installed.
codex.entry.param_neg.deep: CFG negative conditioning. Same syntax as positive (emphasis, BREAK, wildcards). Applied as the unconditional direction the model steers away from during each denoising step. Overly aggressive negatives reduce image quality — the model spends guidance budget avoiding things rather than building what you asked for.
codex.entry.param_cfg.title: CFG Scale
codex.entry.param_cfg.content:
Controls how closely the AI follows your prompt. Higher values = more literal but can oversaturate. Lower values = more creative freedom.

Recommended ranges by architecture:

• SD 1.5: 7–11

• SDXL / Illustrious: 5–7

• Flux: 3.5–5

• Distilled models: 1.0 (guidance is baked into the distillation)

If your images look artificial, oversaturated, or have harsh colors, try lowering CFG first — it’s the most common fix.
codex.entry.param_steps.title: Steps
codex.entry.param_steps.content:
How many refinement passes the AI makes. More steps = more detail but takes longer.

Sweet spot: 20–30. Use 15–20 when experimenting, 28–35 for polished finals. Above 40 rarely helps with most samplers.
codex.entry.param_steps.deep: Diminishing returns above ~30 for most samplers. DPM++ 2M SDE and Euler converge faster than ancestral samplers. Ancestral samplers (anything with "a" in the name) never fully converge — results change with every step count increment.
codex.entry.param_denoise.title: Denoise Strength
codex.entry.param_denoise.content:
Controls how much the AI changes what’s already on the canvas. Only matters when the canvas has content (img2img mode).

• 1.0 — full replace. Only prompt matters.

• 0.7–0.8 — major changes. Good for rough sketches.

• 0.4–0.6 — moderate. Adjusts while keeping structure.

• 0.2–0.3 — gentle. Refines details without altering composition.

Start high and lower it as you get closer to what you want.
codex.entry.param_denoise.deep: Denoise maps to how many steps actually execute: 0.7 at 30 steps = 21 actual denoising steps. Auto-routing: a blank canvas (including one you painted on and then erased) → txt2img, canvas with content → img2img, a selected mask → inpainting.
codex.entry.param_sampler.title: Sampler & Scheduler
codex.entry.param_sampler.content:
The sampler controls the denoising algorithm. The scheduler controls how noise decreases across steps.

Recommended starting points:

• SD 1.5 / SDXL / Illustrious: Euler a or DPM++ 2M SDE + Karras

• Flux: Euler

• Distilled models: Euler (4–8 steps)

Don’t stress about this early on — the difference is often subtle between samplers at the same step count.

Ancestral vs non-ancestral: Samplers with "a" in the name (Euler a, DPM++ 2S a) are ancestral — they add randomness each step, producing more variety but never converging to a stable result. Non-ancestral samplers (DPM++ 2M, Euler) converge asymptotically — results stabilize as step count increases.
codex.entry.param_sampler.deep: All Forge samplers available including bundled custom samplers: BFS (Bandwise Flow), Cacophony, Labyrinth, Parasite, Parasitic BFS, Grimoire, Adams-Bashforth. Custom "Toxic" scheduler uses a φ³ power curve with progressive Karras blending.
codex.entry.param_dimensions.title: Canvas Dimensions
codex.entry.param_dimensions.content:
Base buttons (512–1024) set the overall resolution. Ratio buttons set the shape (square, wide, tall). The ⇄ button swaps orientation.

Recommended resolutions:

• SDXL / Illustrious: 1024×1024 square. For portrait: 832×1216. For landscape: 1216×832.

• SD 1.5: 512×512 or 768×768. Non-square: 512×768, 768×512.

• Flux: 1024×1024 standard.

Going far below or above the model’s native resolution without HiRes Fix can produce artifacts — duplicate limbs, distorted compositions. Use HiRes Fix for large, detailed output rather than generating at high resolution directly.

Bigger images take more VRAM and longer to generate.
codex.entry.loras.title: LoRAs
codex.entry.loras.content:
What are LoRAs? Small add-on files that teach an existing model new things — a specific art style, a character’s face, a type of clothing. They’re much smaller than full models (typically 10–200 MB vs 2–7 GB) and you can stack multiple at once.

Finding LoRAs: Browse CivitAI and filter by "LoRA" type. Check that the model family matches your checkpoint. Read the description for trigger words — many LoRAs require a specific word in your prompt to activate.

Installing: Download the .safetensors file and put it in your LoRA folder (set in Settings → General → Model folders). Use the refresh button to list new files — no restart.

Using: Press + LoRAs under the prompt box to open the LoRA browser, and click a card to add it to the LoRAs list. Each row has an on/off switch and a weight. When you press Generate, Studio adds the <lora:filename:weight> tags and the LoRA’s trigger words to your prompt — Preview shows exactly what will be sent. Import moves <lora:…> tags you typed into the list. Typing the tags by hand still works. Each Auto Detail slot has its own list (LoRAs (this slot only)).

Weight guide: 0.3–0.5 = subtle influence. 0.6–0.8 = typical sweet spot. 0.9–1.0 = full strength (can artifact if overtrained). Above 1.0 = risky. When stacking multiple LoRAs, lower individual weights to prevent conflicts.

Common problems: No effect = wrong model family or missing trigger word. Burnt/oversaturated = weight too high. Same face every time = overtrained, lower to 0.3–0.5.
codex.entry.loras.deep: Standard A1111 <lora:name:weight> syntax, applied at generation time by the engine’s LoRA loader — it modifies specific weight matrices in the UNet and/or text encoder. The LoRA browser reads sidecar .json metadata files; cards show trigger words, search matches against them, and clicking a card adds a list row at the preferred weight.
codex.entry.wildcards.title: Wildcards
codex.entry.wildcards.content:
Wildcards insert randomized text into your prompts. Write __wildcard_name__ and Studio replaces it with a random line from a matching text file. Every generation picks a different line, giving you automatic variety.

Creating a wildcard file:

1. Open your wildcard folder — the one set in Settings → Prompts & Metadata → Dynamic Prompts → Wildcard folder.

2. Create a plain text file. The filename becomes the wildcard name (colors.txt → __colors__).

3. Put one option per line.

4. Use it in your prompt: a __colors__ dress in a garden

Folders: Organize wildcards into folders. A file at wildcards/characters/hair.txt is used as __characters/hair__.

Management: The WILDCARD button near the prompt box opens the wildcard browser. The Wildcards tab in the main tab bar provides a full editor with folder tree, file creation, editing, and preview.
codex.entry.inpaint_basics.title: How to Edit Parts of Your Image
codex.entry.inpaint_basics.content:
Inpainting lets you selectively change parts of an image while keeping the rest untouched. It’s one of the most powerful and commonly used features in Studio.

Step by step:

1. Have an image on your canvas (generate one or load one).

2. Press Q or click the Inpaint Mask tool in the toolstrip. Your brush now paints a red overlay instead of color.

3. Paint red over the area you want to change. − Subtract in the bar above the canvas erases; Clear mask starts over.

4. Write a prompt describing what should appear in the masked area.

5. Hit Generate. Only the red area changes.

6. Press Q again to go back to painting.

More than one mask: the Inpaint mask is a single hard-edged brush mask. For soft edges, or masks made from a selection, from tones or colour, or from prompt words, use named masks. The mask selected in the Masks panel is the one Generate inpaints with — see Masks Panel.

Only Masked vs Whole Picture (the Area menu above the canvas; Only Masked is the default):

Whole Picture generates the full canvas at your set resolution. The AI sees everything and the result blends naturally. Use for: removing objects, changing backgrounds, anything where context matters.

Only Masked crops just the masked region, scales it up, generates, then composites back. Much more detail for small areas. Use for: fixing faces, refining details. Increase the Padding so the AI sees context around the mask.

Fill mode — what goes under the mask:

• Original — keeps existing pixels as the starting point. Best for most tasks.

• Fill — replaces with solid average color. Best for removing objects — the AI fills naturally instead of building on top.

• Latent Nothing — an empty start: more creative freedom, less predictable.

Denoise guide:

• 0.3–0.5 — subtle refinement, artifact cleanup.

• 0.5–0.7 — moderate reshaping.

• 0.7–0.9 — major replacement.

• 1.0 — complete replacement, nothing preserved.

Blur: Softens the mask edge. Higher values (8–16) = smoother transitions. Use 0 for hard cuts.

Common recipes:

• Fix a face: Only Masked + Original + Padding 64–128 + Denoise 0.4–0.6.

• Remove an object: Whole Picture + Fill + Denoise 0.7–0.9. Describe the replacement. For a small blemish, Smart Patch needs no model at all.

• Add something new: Original + Denoise 0.7–0.9. Describe the addition.

• Extend the picture: use Outpaint (see Outpaint & Canvas Size).
codex.entry.inpaint_basics.deep:
The Inpaint mask is a separate canvas buffer, not a layer; named masks live in the Masks panel. “Only Masked” with padding = A1111’s “Inpaint at full resolution” — crops the masked region plus padding, scales to the generation resolution, generates, composites back with mask feathering.

Soft Inpainting (its section appears when the mask tool is active) modifies the pipeline for smooth boundary blending. Parameters: Schedule Bias, Preservation, Contrast Boost, Mask Influence, Diff Threshold, Diff Contrast. With Soft Inpainting on, a soft named mask’s grey is used; with it off, a soft mask is cut at 40%. Adds processing overhead.
codex.entry.masks_panel.title: Masks Panel
codex.entry.masks_panel.content:
Besides the Inpaint mask, a document can hold any number of named masks. They live in the Masks panel, inside Layers.

The list: the first row, Inpaint, is the generation mask you paint with the Inpaint Mask tool; named masks follow. Click a row to select it (this also picks the mask tool). Double-click a name to rename it, click the eye to hide its overlay, click the swatch to change its colour.

Buttons: New mask; Save selection as mask; From range… and From word… (see Masks From Words, Tones & Colour); Load as selection; Duplicate; Invert; Delete (on the Inpaint row it clears the mask instead).

Load as selection: turns the selected mask into a selection. Shift adds to the current selection, Alt subtracts, Shift+Alt intersects. Ctrl+click on a row does the same.

Soft and hard: the Inpaint mask is always a hard brush (size and smoothing only). A named mask’s brush takes Opacity and Hardness, so it can be feathered.

Inpainting with any mask: the mask selected in the panel is the one Generate inpaints with — the selected row says used for inpainting. A soft mask is cut at 40%. With Soft Inpainting on, a feathered mask’s grey is used instead.

Kept for you: masks belong to the tab, survive switching tabs and come back after a reload. When you export a PSD, named masks are saved as layer masks and come back when the PSD is opened in Studio. Develop can also use a named mask for local adjustments.
codex.entry.masks_from_words.title: Masks From Words, Tones & Colour
codex.entry.masks_from_words.content:
A named mask can be made from the picture itself — from its tones, a colour, or a word of the prompt that made it.

From range… (Masks panel). Makes one soft mask from the picture you see: its Highlights, Midtones or Shadows, or a Colour range around the current foreground colour (you choose how far from the colour still counts, 1–255). Nothing is painted.

From word… lists the words of the selected layer’s picture, with strength bars. It needs a picture Studio made with Keep word heatmap data on (Settings → Output & Files → Heatmap data; recorded for Anima and SDXL pictures).

Pick one or more words, then choose the shape: Object (crisp edge — a person, a candle, a sun), Area / light (soft — sky, glow, reflections) or Everything else (all but the picture’s objects — the room, the background). Grow and Feather adjust the edge; you can step through an object’s parts or click to choose the thing yourself.

The first time for a picture takes a few seconds on the CPU, with a progress bar. The first start after the 2026-10-18 update downloads one 41 MB file (MobileSAM) for this.

A word mask remembers its recipe: its ↻ button remakes it from the same words on another picture. The Gallery’s Words section (see Word Heatmaps) can start a mask from a word too.
codex.entry.outpaint_canvas_size.title: Outpaint & Canvas Size
codex.entry.outpaint_canvas_size.content:
Both live in the canvas right-click menu (see Canvas Right-Click Menu), not on a toolbar.

Canvas Size… grows or trims the document around an anchor (the 3×3 grid picks which edge or corner stays put). Nothing is scaled: new space is transparent, and a smaller size trims. Sizes are rounded to a multiple of 8.

Outpaint… makes the picture bigger and asks the model to paint the new space:

1. Choose how far to extend each side — Left, Right, Top, Bottom, in pixels (rounded to a multiple of 8).

2. Overlap into the picture is how much of the existing edge is repainted so the join is seamless.

3. Refine new area adds a second, light pass over the new area at full detail — crisper, slower, and off unless you choose it (it is remembered).

4. Press Extend. Studio fills the new area from the picture’s edge on a layer called Outpaint fill, masks it plus the overlap, and sets up inpainting. The width and height boxes update.

5. Describe what should appear and press Generate. Your inpaint settings are used as they are.

Outpainting takes about as long as one normal generation, even on large pictures.
codex.entry.hires_fix.title: HiRes Fix
codex.entry.hires_fix.content:
Two-pass generation: generates at normal size first, then upscales and adds detail. Produces much sharper results than generating at large resolution directly.

Scale: enlargement factor (2.0 = double dimensions).

Denoise: 0.2–0.4 for detail without changing content. Higher values reshape more.

Steps: 0 = same as first pass.

Upscaler: "Latent" = smooth/painterly feel. R-ESRGAN = sharp/detailed.

Advanced: a separate CFG and a different checkpoint for the second pass.

On Anima the Hires pass runs at the same shift as the base pass (as Forge Neo does), so Anima pictures made with Hires before the 2026-10-18 update differ slightly.
codex.entry.hires_fix.deep: Base resolution → latent or pixel upscale → img2img at scaled resolution. Separate CFG and checkpoint overrides available for the second pass. Output dimensions = base × scale; UI restores base dims after generation. HiRes + ADetailer = multiplicative cost — each adds a full pass.
codex.entry.adetailer.title: ADetailer
codex.entry.adetailer.content:
Automatically detects faces (and optionally hands/bodies) in your generated image and regenerates them at higher detail. Fixes the most common AI problem — faces looking wrong or blurry at smaller sizes.

3 slots. Slot 1 is set up for faces. Enable a slot’s checkbox and it runs automatically after generation (after Hires, if both are on).

Each slot has its own Model (the detector — or Words…, see below), Confidence (how sure the detector must be), Denoise (how much to change), Mask Blur, a Prompt (blank = the main prompt; describe the face specifically) and its own LoRAs (this slot only).

Word Detail: choose Words… as a slot’s model to detail the prompt words you name instead of a detected face. See Auto Detail: Word Detail.

While you inpaint, faces the mask doesn’t cover are skipped, so a face fix doesn’t repaint the rest of the picture.
codex.entry.adetailer.deep: Post-generation YOLO-based detection + inpainting pipeline. Per-slot flow: detect → crop region → inpaint at higher resolution → composite back. Five detectors are bundled (faces, hands and people). Each region gets its own seed and the detector’s order is kept, as ADetailer does; [SEP] and [PROMPT] work in slot prompts. Runs after Hires Fix if both are enabled.
codex.entry.word_detail.title: Auto Detail: Word Detail
codex.entry.word_detail.content:
An Auto Detail slot can detail prompt words instead of a detected face. In the slot, choose Words… as the Model and type the words to detail in the Words field. Studio uses the picture’s own heatmap data to find where each word landed, then repaints just those regions with the slot’s Denoise, Mask Blur and Prompt.

It needs heatmap recording on (Settings → Output & Files → Heatmap data). In a batch, only the first picture — the one with word data — is detailed.

Use it for things a face detector can’t find: the sword, the necklace, the eyes.
codex.entry.develop.title: Develop
codex.entry.develop.content:
The Develop tab adjusts how the picture looks — light, colour and detail — with sliders. The switch beside the title turns Develop on and off without losing your settings; B/A flips between before and after; Reset clears every adjustment. While the Develop panel is showing, Ctrl+Z undoes Develop steps.

Global sliders: a Calibrate group (White Balance, White Point and Black Point eyedroppers, Temperature, Tint), then Exposure, Contrast, Highlights, Shadows, Whites, Blacks, Vibrance and Saturation, and further sections for HSL / Color, Color Grading, Tone Curve and Detail. Saved Develop presets work.

Local adjustments: adjust part of the picture through a named mask. Make the mask first (Masks panel, From range…, From word…), then press Add local adjustment in the Develop tab, choose the mask there, and move Exposure, Contrast, Highlights, Shadows, Whites, Blacks, Temperature, Tint, Saturation or Vibrance — they change only what the mask covers. Choosing a mask for Develop does not change which mask Generate inpaints with.

Develop works on ordinary 8-bit pictures; there is no High Precision (float) source.
codex.entry.layers_basics.title: Working with Layers
codex.entry.layers_basics.content:
1 — Composite in passes. Generate a base, send it to the canvas, add a layer, mask the area you want to change, and regenerate just that region. Repeat to build the image element by element — background first, then a character, then details. If your instinct is “background first, then the character,” that instinct is right — the spelling is mask + regenerate, not per-layer generation.

2 — Paint-over correction. Paint fixes on a layer above the image — rough shapes, color blocks, redraws — then inpaint through them: mask the painted area and regenerate at moderate denoise so your strokes become finished detail.

Layers are transparent sheets stacked on each other. + adds a new layer, ▲▼ reorder, ⇩ merge down, the eye toggles visibility. Each layer has its own Opacity and Blend Mode (Normal, Multiply, Screen, Overlay, Soft Light, Hard Light, Difference, …); Merge Down composites using the current blend mode and opacity.

The buttons beside them add adjustment layers (Brightness/Contrast, Hue/Saturation, Levels) that change everything beneath them without touching the pixels. Below the layer list, the Masks panel holds named masks (see Masks Panel) and the History panel lists every undo step.

Generated images land on the reference layer (bottom); your painting goes on paint layers above, so regenerating never destroys painted edits — they live on a different layer.
codex.entry.psd_export.title: PSD Export
codex.entry.psd_export.content:
Export your full layer stack as a PSD file that opens in Photoshop, Krita, GIMP, or any PSD-compatible editor. Click the Save Canvas / PSD button (the disk icon above the layer list).

Layer names, blend modes, opacity, and visibility are all preserved. You can continue working in your preferred editor without losing your stack.

Named masks are saved as PSD layer masks and come back when the PSD is opened in Studio.
codex.entry.psd_export.deep: Built via ag-psd.js. Served via dedicated FastAPI route. Firefox uses POST + download (no showSaveFilePicker support).
codex.entry.gallery_overview.title: Gallery
codex.entry.gallery_overview.content:
Gallery is Studio’s image library. It browses the pictures in the folders you link — your Studio results and any other folder of images.

Getting started: the Gallery shows the folders you link. Press Choose folder & scan to link one — your Studio results folder, or any folder full of images — and it scans everything in it. Studio also links its own results folder by itself when it exists. You can link more folders later via Link new folder at the bottom of the sidebar.

Layout:

• Left sidebar — folder tree on top, character tag list below. Drag the column divider to resize. Click a folder or tag to filter; click again to clear.

• Top bar — search box and sort controls. Search matches filenames, character tags, and embedded metadata (prompt text, models, LoRAs). Autocomplete suggests known tags and metadata words as you type. Sort by filename, newest or oldest, or folder — click a sort button again to flip direction.

• Main grid — your images, infinite-scrolling. Click any image for the detail view.

Character tags: Gallery auto-parses character names out of filenames using common patterns (underscores and dashes connect name parts, commas and plus signs separate characters). A file named John_Doe+Jane_Smith_seed123.png becomes tagged with John Doe and Jane Smith. The tag list in the sidebar groups tags by first letter.

You can manually add or remove tags per image from the detail view. See Gallery Settings in Gallery itself for the full tagging rules and the ignore words list (words that never become tags, like "seed" or "sample").

Detail view: Click any image. You get full resolution, embedded metadata (prompt, settings, seed, LoRAs, sampler, everything stored in the PNG), character tags (editable), filename (editable), a Words section (see Word Heatmaps), and action buttons for send-to-canvas, rename, move, delete, and open-in-explorer. Arrow keys navigate to adjacent images without closing the view. Send to Folio appears only where Folio is installed.

Updates: pictures Studio saves appear in the grid on their own, a moment after they are written. The dot in the top bar shows whether Studio is also watching your folders for files added, moved or deleted outside Studio — green when it is, grey when it isn’t. Watching needs an optional file-watching component; without it, rescan by hand to pick up outside changes.

Send to Canvas: Load any Gallery image onto your Studio canvas for editing. Also reads the embedded metadata — prompt, seed, and settings get restored so you can iterate from there. In Gallery Settings you choose which prompt version is applied: raw (with wildcards) or resolved (what the model saw).
codex.entry.gallery_overview.deep: Built on TrackImage by Moritz, integrated as Studio’s Gallery module. Multi-folder scanning via linked scan folders. Real-time updates via SSE at /studio/gallery/events; Studio’s own saves trigger a scan directly (no filesystem watcher needed), outside changes need watchdog. suppress_path() prevents duplicate events on rename/move/delete. SQLite backend with PRAGMA busy_timeout=30000 for lock contention. Autocomplete endpoint at /suggest; metadata extracted from SD/ComfyUI/EXIF headers into an indexed search_text column. Video files get thumbnails via ffmpeg. Perceptual hashes (a built-in 64×64 DCT hash) power the duplicate detector.
codex.entry.gallery_organize.title: Organizing Images
codex.entry.gallery_organize.content:
Gallery supports bulk operations on multiple images at once. Everything is undoable.

Selection:

• Click an image — selects just that one.

• Ctrl+Click — toggles individual images in and out of the selection.

• Shift+Click — selects a range between the last-clicked image and the one you shift-click.

• A selection bar appears at the top of the grid showing the count and the bulk-action buttons.

Bulk rename: Pick a base name; Gallery numbers multiple files automatically. Use underscores for multi-word character names and commas or plus signs to separate characters — John_Doe+Jane_Smith produces files that Gallery re-parses as two separate character tags. If a filename collision happens, Gallery offers to auto-increment or overwrite.

Bulk move: Drag selected images onto any folder in the sidebar to move them there. You can also use the Move button in the selection bar to pick a destination from a folder picker. Both are undoable — Ctrl+Z moves everything back.

Bulk delete: Deleted images go to Gallery’s trash — they’re not hard-deleted immediately. Ctrl+Z restores them. Trash is per-Gallery, separate from the OS recycle bin.

Clipboard: Cut or copy a selection, then paste into a different folder — like file manager clipboard semantics, but scoped to Gallery. Cut moves, copy duplicates.

Format conversion: Convert selected images between PNG, JPEG, and WebP. For formats without alpha (JPEG), you pick how transparency is handled — skip transparent files, or flatten to white or black. Option to keep originals or replace them. Option to strip in-file metadata during conversion.

Strip metadata: Removes embedded EXIF / PNG metadata from the files on disk. Generation parameters stored in the Gallery database are preserved — the detail-view metadata panel keeps working. Use this before sharing images publicly if you don’t want your prompt and settings going out with them.

Tag editing (bulk): The Tags button in the selection bar opens a bulk tag editor. Shows tags that are common to all selected images, tags that only some have (with a count like 3/5), and lets you add or remove tags across the whole selection at once.

Undo: Ctrl+Z reverses the last Gallery operation — rename, move, delete, copy. The undo stack persists through the current session.

Context menu: Right-click an image for the same actions (rename, move, delete, strip metadata, send to canvas, open in explorer). Right-click a folder in the sidebar for folder-level actions (rename, unlink — which removes the link without deleting files on disk).
codex.entry.gallery_words.title: Word Heatmaps
codex.entry.gallery_words.content:
When Keep word heatmap data is on (Settings → Output & Files → Heatmap data), Anima and SDXL pictures record where each prompt word landed while the image was generated. It adds about half a second and a small file per picture; turn it off for big batches.

In the Gallery’s detail view, the Words section lists the prompt’s words. Click a word to see where it landed in the picture; the strength note compares it with the picture’s typical word. Text used here shows where the picture drew on the prompt at all — dark areas were left to the model.

A word can start a mask (From word…, see Masks From Words, Tones & Colour) or a Word Detail slot (see Auto Detail: Word Detail).

The same settings card lets you move the heatmap data to another folder or clean up files whose pictures are gone. Recording does not change the pictures themselves.
codex.entry.gallery_duplicates.title: Finding Duplicates
codex.entry.gallery_duplicates.content:
Gallery can find visually similar images across your library — not just exact file duplicates, but images that look the same. Useful when you’ve generated the same concept repeatedly with different seeds, or ended up with near-identical outputs you forgot about.

Running a scan: Open the duplicates view from the Gallery topbar (Find duplicates). Pictures that have no fingerprint yet are hashed first (Compute hashes; the dialog shows “N / total images hashed”) — this can take a while on a large library, but each picture is only hashed once. Then pick a Similarity threshold (stricter = only near-identical, looser = minor edits count; up to 25% difference) and press Scan for duplicates.

Results view: Duplicates appear as groups. Each group shows the similar files side by side with thumbnails, filenames, and folder paths. A header shows the total — e.g. "12 groups · 38 files (keeping one per group would free 26 files)".

Review and delete:

• Each file has a checkbox. Check the ones you want to delete.

• Each group has a Select all but first button — fastest way to keep one copy per group and trash the rest.

• Deletions go to Gallery trash, undoable with Ctrl+Z. If you decide you wanted one back, undo restores it.

What counts as "similar": Perceptual hashing is tolerant of minor differences — small crops, compression, slight color shifts — so cropped and re-saved versions of the same image still cluster. It’s not semantic similarity — two different generations of "a red cat" won’t group unless they came out genuinely close-looking.
codex.entry.workshop_overview.title: Workshop
codex.entry.workshop_overview.content:
Workshop is Studio’s model crafting suite. It lets you build new checkpoints by combining existing ones, bake LoRAs and VAEs into checkpoints permanently, and chain several steps together in one recipe.

What you can do:

• Merge two or three checkpoints with Weighted Sum, SLERP or Add Difference, optionally with block weights.

• Bake LoRAs directly into a checkpoint so you don’t need to load them separately.

• Bake a VAE into a checkpoint so you don’t need to pick one.

• Chain rows as a recipe — merge A and B, bake a LoRA into the result, swap the VAE, save. One recipe, one output.

• Inspect models: a basic Inspector shows a model’s info, A/B compatibility and a memory check before you start.

Running it: build your recipe on the merge board and press Begin Merge. The result is written as a new .safetensors in your first checkpoint folder. An existing file is never overwritten, and a cancelled run leaves nothing half-written.

Trying a merge in memory first (“Test Merge”) and the extra merge methods are not available — see Not in Studio Yet.

Every completed merge or bake logs to the History tab (see Journal & Recipes) with its full recipe, so you can reproduce any experiment later.
codex.entry.workshop_methods.title: Merge Methods
codex.entry.workshop_methods.content:
Workshop offers three merge methods. Pick based on what you’re trying to achieve, not by instinct — the differences are real.

Basic blending:

• Weighted Sum — linear interpolation between A and B per alpha. Simplest, fastest, always works. Start here.

• SLERP — spherical interpolation. Preserves the magnitude of weight vectors instead of averaging them. Usually produces sharper, more vibrant results than Weighted Sum at the same alpha. Best when blending two models of similar quality.

Training transplant:

• Add Difference — extracts what B learned relative to its base model C, then applies that training to A. Use this to transplant a finetune’s skills (e.g. anime style, specific subject) into a different model. Requires Model C — the base B was finetuned from.

When in doubt: Weighted Sum 0.5 is always a reasonable baseline. If results look washed out, try SLERP next. If you’re merging a specific finetune of a known base, use Add Difference.
codex.entry.workshop_block_weights.title: Block Weights
codex.entry.workshop_block_weights.conte:
Instead of merging every layer of the model at the same alpha, block weights let you assign different alphas to different parts of the UNet. This gives you much finer control over what gets merged where.

Block structure (SDXL):

• Input blocks — early layers process the noisy latent. Later input blocks handle structural features, composition, and layout.
