• Middle — the bottleneck. Most compressed representation of the image, the model’s core understanding. Affects global coherence.

• Output blocks — expand back to full resolution. Early output blocks = structure, later = fine details and rendering quality.

Common patterns:

• Keep A’s composition, use B’s rendering — low alpha on input and middle blocks, high alpha on late output blocks.

• Keep A’s style, use B’s subject knowledge — opposite: high alpha on input/middle, low on output.

• Transplant faces only — very localized block weights on the blocks that tend to encode face features.

Block weights work with all three merge methods; switch them on per row with the row’s blocks toggle.
codex.entry.workshop_lora_bake.title: LoRA Baking
codex.entry.workshop_lora_bake.content:
LoRA baking permanently merges a LoRA (or several) into a checkpoint. The result is a single .safetensors file that behaves as if the LoRA is always active at the baked strength — no <lora:...> tags needed.

When to bake instead of loading as a LoRA:

• You always use this LoRA with this checkpoint.

• You want to distribute the result as a self-contained model.

• You’re stacking multiple LoRAs and want a simpler runtime setup.

• You want the LoRA’s effect at a weight not expressible at load time (e.g. bake at 0.7 plus another at 0.4 for a specific blend).

Supported adapter types: LoRA, LoHa, LoKr, OFT, BOFT, GLoRA, DoRA, plus raw diff and set patches. Studio auto-detects the adapter type per file from its key suffixes — you don’t have to tell it what kind of LoRA you’re baking.

Tips:

• Bake at a strength you’ve tested first. There’s no slider at runtime after baking — you’re locked in.

• Architecture must match. An SDXL LoRA won’t bake into an SD 1.5 checkpoint.

• Multiple LoRAs in a recipe are applied sequentially, so order can matter for non-linear adapter types.
codex.entry.workshop_lora_bake.deep: All math performed in fp32 to avoid precision loss, downcast only at save. VAE keys always stay fp32 regardless of checkpoint format. Key matching uses four strategies: the standard Kohya lora_unet_*/lora_te*_* prefix convention, Flux/SD3 direct format, generic base.weight matching, and a full CompVis↔diffusers prefix table for SDXL diffusers-format LoRAs. DoRA decomposition is detected via dora_scale keys and applied via the standard weight-norm rescaling after the delta is added.
codex.entry.workshop_vae_bake.title: VAE Baking
codex.entry.workshop_vae_bake.content:
VAE baking replaces the VAE embedded in a checkpoint with a different one. The result is a checkpoint that always uses the new VAE — users don’t have to pick one from the dropdown.

When to use it:

• Your favorite checkpoint has baked-in color/saturation issues and a specific VAE fixes them (e.g. vae-ft-mse-840000 on many SD 1.5 checkpoints).

• You’re distributing a checkpoint and want it to "just work" without VAE setup.

• You’re building a self-contained recipe with merges, LoRA bakes, and a specific VAE all rolled into one file.

VAE architecture must match checkpoint architecture. SDXL VAE into SD 1.5 checkpoint won’t work.
codex.entry.workshop_journal.title: Journal & Recipes
codex.entry.workshop_journal.content:
Every completed merge, LoRA bake, VAE bake, and chain run auto-logs to the History tab with its full recipe. You get a searchable history of every experiment you’ve ever run.

Per-entry:

• Full recipe (method, alpha, models involved, block weights, parameters).

• Timestamp and elapsed time.

• Editable rating (0–5 stars), tags, and notes.

• Optional sample image — attach a test generation to remember what this merge actually looked like.

Search & filter: by text (searches name, notes, and recipe contents), by tag, or by type (merge / LoRA bake / VAE bake / note). You can also add manual notes for models you didn’t make in Workshop but want to track.

Recipes are saved chain configurations — a sequence of merge/bake steps that reference previous step outputs as __O1__, __O2__, etc. Import a past recipe from History back onto the merge board to run it again with different models. Intermediate outputs are auto-deleted unless you check Keep intermediates.
codex.entry.common_problems.title: Common Problems
codex.entry.common_problems.content:
Black image: Model didn’t load or VRAM ran out. Check the Jobs block for the reason, reduce dimensions, or turn off Hires Fix.

Garbled/noisy result: CFG too high or wrong model for your settings. Lower CFG to 5–7. SDXL models need at least 768×768.

Generation is very slow: Steps + HiRes Fix + ADetailer are multiplicative. Each adds a full pass. Disable what you don’t need.

Nothing happens when you press Generate: Studio needs a model chosen first (and, for some families, a text encoder and VAE). The Jobs block says what is missing — see Models & VAE.

First image after changing the model is slow: Generate loads the model you chose. Later images reuse it.

Same image every time: Your seed is locked. Check the Seed field — if it’s not -1, click the dice button to re-enable random seeds.

Wrong colors / washed out: Try a different VAE in the dropdown.

"Disconnected" in status bar: WebSocket dropped. Refresh the page. If persistent, check the console window Studio was started from for errors.

Extra fingers / bad anatomy: Common AI artifact. Use ADetailer for faces. Add "bad hands, extra fingers" to negatives. Inpaint specific problem areas manually.

LoRA has no effect: Model family mismatch (a LoRA made for another family), missing trigger word, or weight too low.
codex.entry.vram_management.title: VRAM & Performance
codex.entry.vram_management.content:
VRAM is your GPU’s memory. The loaded model is the biggest user. If generation is slow or stops with a memory error:

• Use smaller dimensions.

• Turn off Hires Fix and any Auto Detail slots you don’t need — steps, Hires and Auto Detail each add a pass, and they multiply.

• Make several images as separate queued jobs rather than one huge one.

Settings → Performance & VRAM:

• GPU — which graphics card Studio uses on a machine with more than one. Takes effect at the next start.

• GPU Weights — how much VRAM to use for model weights (0 = the engine’s own default). Higher keeps more of the model on the GPU for speed; lower frees VRAM for the generation itself.

• Unload Model from VRAM frees the GPU now; Auto-unload when idle does it after the Idle timeout. The model reloads on the next Generate. Feature suggested by SnekySnek.

• Use GPU tile compositing — blends upscaler tiles on the GPU. Faster upscales; pixel values can differ very slightly.

Advanced launch options are listed as comments in Start-Studio.bat (attention backend, memory allocator, offload streams, fast fp16, a timing log). Studio picks sensible defaults; change them only to diagnose a problem or to force something. Some change the image itself — the file says which.

Everything else — CFG, Steps, Seed, Sampler — you’ll learn by experimenting. The Codex tab explains each one when you’re ready.
education.tour.core.revealWorkspace.text: Toolstrip (left) — 19 painting tools. Start with B for brush and E for eraser. Layers (right panel) — generated images land on the bottom layer, your painting goes above. Regenerating never destroys your painted edits. This is a real canvas. Paint, generate, paint more, generate again.
education.tour.core.welcome.text: Welcome to Forge Studio. Let’s make your first image. See the text box on the right? Describe something you’d like to see — anything at all.
education.tour.experienced.canvasRouting: No separate txt2img/img2img tabs. Studio checks the canvas and routes automatically: • Blank canvas → txt2img • Content on canvas → img2img • Mask painted → inpainting The pixels are the source of truth. Paint something, erase it all, generate — that’s txt2img because the canvas is blank. No mode toggles.
education.tour.experienced.canvasUx.text: A few things that work differently here: • Context bar values are scrub labels — drag horizontally to adjust, click to type a number. • Each tool remembers its own settings independently. Switch tools and back — settings preserved. • Shift+Drag on canvas adjusts brush size (horizontal) and opacity (vertical). • Ctrl+Click eyedrops from any tool without switching. • At 200%+ zoom, pixels render nearest-neighbor (crisp, not blurry).
education.tour.experienced.extras.text: Auto Detail (3 slots, including a Words detector) runs automatically after generation. Drag and drop an image onto the canvas to load it — resizes canvas, imports metadata, creates a new layer. Save current settings as workflow defaults — persists server-side across sessions — or as named workflows. Model folders, save folders and the file-name pattern are in Settings.
education.tour.experienced.layers.text: Real layer stack with blend modes, opacity, and reordering. Sending results to canvas creates a new layer — never overwrites your work. Generation results go to a reusable "Gen Result" layer. Your painted edits on other layers are always safe. Export the full stack as PSD.
education.tour.experienced.layout.text: Quick orientation. Toolstrip on the left (19 painting tools plus the Inpaint Mask). Canvas in the center — scroll to zoom, Space+drag to pan, right-click for the canvas menu. Panel on the right (Generate and Extensions tabs). \ collapses it. Settings is its own tab at the top. Context bar above the canvas shows controls for the active tool.
education.tour.experienced.maskRegions.t: The Inpaint Mask tool (Q) paints a hard-edged generation mask. Beside it, the Masks panel (inside Layers) holds named masks — from a brush, a selection, tones, a colour or a prompt word — with their own opacity and hardness. The mask selected there is the one Generate inpaints with. There are no separate txt2img/img2img/inpaint tabs: the canvas and the selected mask decide.
education.tour.experienced.shortcuts.tex: Key shortcuts to know: Q Mask mode • B Brush • E Eraser • V Transform [/] Brush size • Shift+Drag Size + opacity Ctrl+Enter Generate • \ Toggle panel Ctrl+Z Undo • Space+Drag Pan • Scroll Zoom Full list in the Codex tab (highlighted above) under Keyboard Shortcuts. You’re set. Go make something.
education.tour.inpaint.masking.text: What if you only want to change part of the image? Press Q to pick the Inpaint Mask tool. Your brush now paints a red overlay. The red tells the AI: "only change this area." Paint the mask → write what should go there → Generate. Only the masked area changes. Press Q again to go back to painting. You’ll use this constantly.
education.tour.inpaint.paint.text: Your image is on the canvas now — ready to work with. Pick up the brush (B) and paint something on top of it. Scribble, add a shape, change a color. Don’t worry about being precise.
education.tour.inpaint.regenerate.text: Now hit Generate again. The AI sees your paint strokes and incorporates them. It reinterprets the whole canvas with your edits as input — not just pasting paint on top. The Denoise slider controls how much it changes. Lower = keep more of what’s there.
education.tour.modelBranch.needModel.tex: Before we start, Studio needs an AI model — the brain that generates images — and it can’t see one yet. If you don’t have one, here’s a good starter: Download ToxicHost’s recommended model Save it in a folder of your own. Then open Settings → General → Model folders, add that folder as the Checkpoint folder (use Browse…) and press Save folders. The Setting Up Models article in the Codex has the details.
education.tour.modelBranch.refreshModels: Now click the refresh button (↻) next to the Model dropdown. Studio will rescan your folders without needing a restart. Once your model appears in the dropdown, select it and we’ll get started.

help.adetailer.confidence: Minimum detection confidence. Lower finds more regions but risks false positives; 0.3 is typical.
help.adetailer.denoise: How much each detected region is repainted. 0.3–0.5 refines detail without changing identity.
help.adetailer.maskBlur: Softens the edge of each detected region before inpainting so the fix blends into its surroundings.
help.adetailer.model: Detection model that finds regions to refine, such as faces or hands. None disables the slot.
help.adetailer.prompt: Optional prompt used only inside detected regions. Blank uses the main prompt.
help.controlnet.end: Point in the generation (0–1) where control stops. Earlier ends relax control for the final steps.
help.controlnet.mode: Balance between the prompt and the control signal when they disagree.
help.controlnet.model: ControlNet model that applies the control signal. It must match the preprocessor family.
help.controlnet.preprocessor: Converts the source image into the control signal (edges, depth, pose) the ControlNet model expects.
help.controlnet.source: Where the control image comes from: the canvas, the active layer, or an uploaded file.
help.controlnet.start: Point in the generation (0–1) where control begins. Later starts give the prompt more freedom early on.
help.controlnet.weight: How strongly the control signal steers generation. 1.0 is full strength.
help.hires.cfg: Prompt strength for the hires pass. 0 reuses the main CFG.
help.hires.checkpoint: Optional different checkpoint for the hires pass. Same uses the main model.
help.hires.denoise: How much the upscaled image may change during the hires pass. Lower keeps the composition; 0.3–0.5 is typical.
help.hires.scale: Multiplier applied to the base resolution before the hires pass. 1.5–2.0 is typical.
help.hires.steps: Steps for the hires pass. 0 reuses the main step count.
help.hires.upscaler: Upscaler used for the hires pass. Latent upscales inside the model; ESRGAN-style upscalers work on the pixels.
help.sampling.cfg: How strongly the image follows the prompt. Higher values follow it more literally but can oversaturate; 4–8 is typical.
help.sampling.denoise: How much the existing canvas is repainted in img2img. 0 keeps the input, 1 replaces it entirely; 0.4–0.8 balances change and structure.
help.sampling.sampler: Algorithm that steps the image from noise to the final result. Different samplers trade speed, detail, and reproducibility.
help.sampling.scheduler: Controls how denoising effort is distributed across steps. Karras concentrates steps where they matter most and is a safe default.
help.sampling.steps: How many denoising steps to run. More steps add detail with diminishing returns; 20–35 is typical.
help.seed.extra: Shows variation-seed controls for reproducible small variations on a base seed.
help.status.vram: {alloc} GB allocated by tensors · {reserved} GB reserved by PyTorch · {total} GB total. Model weights may be partially offloaded to RAM.
help.upscale.denoise: How much the refine pass may change the upscaled image. Around 0.3 adds detail without drifting.
help.upscale.refine: Runs an img2img pass after upscaling to reconstruct detail. The Steps and Denoise below apply to this pass.
help.upscale.runAD: Runs ADetailer during the refine pass to fix faces and other detected regions.
help.upscale.upscaler: Model used to enlarge the current canvas.

showme.clone.intro.text: See the pink square on the ground? We’ll remove it using the Clone Stamp. This tool copies pixels from one area and paints them over another — perfect for removing unwanted objects.
showme.clone.paint.text: Now paint directly over the pink square. The tool copies green ground from the source point, covering the pink. If the clone starts picking up wrong content, Alt+Click a new source and keep going.
showme.clone.select.text: Press K to select the Clone Stamp tool.
showme.clone.source.text: Now hold Alt and click on a clean area of green ground near the pink square. This sets your source point — where the clone copies from.
showme.dynamics.intro.text: The brush engine has a dynamics panel that controls how a stroke is built. Select the Brush (B) and click the gear icon at the end of the brush presets (highlighted).
showme.dynamics.panel.text: The panel has three groups: • Stroke — Follow stroke, Buildup (stamps accumulate), Spacing, Size / Opacity / Rotation Jitter, Scatter • Brush Shape — Ratio, Density, Spikes, Angle, Taper in, Falloff (Std or Gauss) • Paper — a surface texture (Fine Grain, Canvas, Rough Tooth, Laid) with Depth, Scale and Tooth; it belongs to the document, so every brush paints on the same surface
showme.dynamics.try.text: Try painting with different settings. High scatter + size jitter creates foliage and particle effects. High spacing creates dotted lines. A paper surface makes strokes break up like chalk. The Scatter preset is pre-configured for textured spray. Each preset stores its own dynamics.
showme.inpaint.generate.text: Hit Generate. Only the masked area changes — the rest stays untouched. Afterward, press Q to go back to painting. Try different denoise values to see how much changes.
showme.inpaint.intro.text: Here’s a simple scene. Let’s change part of it using inpainting. See the sun in the sky? We’re going to replace it with something else.
showme.inpaint.mask.text: Press Q to pick the Inpaint Mask tool (highlighted). Your brush now paints a red overlay instead of color. Paint red over the sun. It doesn’t need to be precise — just cover it.
showme.inpaint.prompt.text: A prompt has been pre-filled — "a full moon in a night sky" — but you can change it to whatever you want. The AI will only change the red area.
showme.label: Show Me
showme.layers.blend.text: Each layer has Opacity and Blend Mode. Try changing Layer 1’s blend mode to Multiply or Screen to see how it interacts with the layer below. The Save Canvas / PSD button (the disk icon above the list) exports the full stack as a PSD.
showme.layers.generation.text: When you Generate, the result lands on the reference (bottom) layer. Your painting on upper layers is never overwritten. This means you can always regenerate without losing your edits.
showme.layers.intro.text: This canvas has two layers. The Background layer has a blue square. Layer 1 has a red square overlapping it. Layers are transparent sheets stacked on each other.
showme.layers.visibility.text: Try clicking the eye icon on Layer 1 to hide it. The red square disappears, revealing the blue one underneath. Click it again to show it. This is how you control what’s visible without deleting anything.
showme.lora.browse.text: The browser shows a card for each LoRA file in your LoRA folder (set in Settings → General → Model folders). Cards show the name and trigger words (read from sidecar .json files). Use the search bar to filter by name or trigger word.
showme.lora.insert.text: Click a card to add it to the list at its preferred weight. When you press Generate, Studio adds the <lora:name:weight> tags and any trigger words to the prompt for you — Preview shows exactly what will be sent. You can stack several; lower the weights (0.5–0.7) when you do. Import moves <lora:…> tags you typed into the list.
showme.lora.intro.text: The LoRAs block under the prompt box keeps your LoRAs as a list, so you never type the syntax by hand. Press + LoRAs to open the LoRA browser.
showme.radialSym.enable.text: In the context bar (top of the canvas area), find the symmetry buttons (near the right side). Click the radial button (the starburst icon). Set the axis count — try 6 for a snowflake pattern or 8 for a mandala. More axes = more repetitions.
showme.radialSym.intro.text: Radial symmetry mirrors your brush strokes around a center point. Let’s paint a mandala pattern. First, select the Brush tool (B).
showme.radialSym.paint.text:
Now paint on the canvas. Every stroke is replicated around the center point.

Try painting outward from the center, or in arcs. Even simple strokes create complex patterns.

The smudge tool also works with radial symmetry — each segment has its own independent smudge buffer.
showme.routing.blank.text: This is a blank canvas. If you hit Generate right now, Studio runs txt2img — generating from scratch based only on your prompt. No mode selection needed. The canvas state IS the mode.
showme.routing.content.text: Now paint something on the canvas — anything. A scribble, a shape, a splash of color. Once there are pixels on the canvas, Generate switches to img2img automatically. The AI works with what’s there. Denoise controls how much it changes.
showme.routing.mask.text: Now press Q to pick the Inpaint Mask tool (highlighted) and paint a red overlay over part of your content. A mask selected in the Masks panel counts too. With a mask present, Generate switches to inpainting — only the masked area changes. Everything else stays untouched. Three modes, zero toggles. The pixels decide.
showme.softInpaint.enable.text: Find Soft Inpainting in the Generate panel (it appears when the mask tool is active). Enable the checkbox. Six parameters. The two that matter most: • Preservation — how much of the original is kept. Higher = less change. • Contrast Boost — how sharp the blend edge is. Lower = softer blend.
showme.softInpaint.generate.text: Hit Generate and compare with Soft Inpainting off (same mask, same seed). With Soft Inpainting on, the mask’s grey is used; with it off, a soft mask is cut at 40%. The other parameters (Schedule Bias, Mask Influence, Diff Threshold/Contrast) are fine at their defaults until you need specific control.
showme.softInpaint.intro.text: Standard inpainting has a hard boundary — inside the mask changes, outside doesn’t. Soft Inpainting blends smoothly across the boundary for more natural transitions. It works with a soft mask, and the Inpaint Mask is always a hard brush. So make a named mask: click New mask in the Masks panel.
showme.transform.basic.text: Try the basics: drag a corner handle to resize. Hold Shift to constrain proportions. Drag inside to reposition. Enter applies the transform. Escape cancels.
showme.transform.intro.text: Here’s a shape on the canvas. Press V to activate the Transform tool. Drag the handles to resize, drag inside to move, and rotate from the corners.
showme.transform.warp.text: The bar above the canvas has more modes: • Skew (K) — edge handles shear the shape • Persp (P) — drag the corners freely for perspective • Warp (W) — free deformation with control points; then Aff, Sim or Rig picks how it deforms (affine, angle-preserving, shape-preserving) There are also Flip and Rotate buttons. Try each one.
showme.wildcards.browse.text: Click the WILDCARD button under the prompt box to open the wildcard browser. It lists your wildcard files. They live in the wildcard folder you choose in Settings → Prompts & Metadata → Dynamic Prompts. Each .txt file is one wildcard — the filename becomes the name.
showme.wildcards.intro.text: Wildcards insert random text into your prompts for automatic variety. The syntax is __name__ (double underscores). Each generation picks a different line from the matching text file.
showme.wildcards.lexicon.text: The Wildcards tab (in the main tab bar) is a full wildcard editor — folder tree, file creation, inline editing, preview, sorting and duplicate removal. Wildcards work in the negative prompt too. Common pattern: put your standard negatives in neg4.txt and use __neg4__ instead of typing them every time.
showme.wildcards.syntax.text: Try typing in your prompt: a __colors__ cat sitting on a __furniture__ Each generation replaces __colors__ with a random line from colors.txt and __furniture__ from furniture.txt. Folders work too: a file at animals/cats.txt is used as __animals/cats__.

workshop.method.add_difference.desc: Extracts what Model B learned from Model C (its base), then applies that training to Model A. Use this to transplant a finetune's skills (e.g. anime style, specific subject) into a different model. Requires Model C — the base model B was finetuned from.
workshop.method.breadcrumbs.desc: Dual-threshold trimming — like TIES but also removes the largest outlier changes, not just the smallest. Density controls the lower cutoff (how much to keep), Drop Rate controls the upper cutoff (how many outliers to remove). Best for finetunes with both noise and overfitting artifacts.
workshop.method.cosine_adaptive.desc: Automatically computes a unique blend ratio for every weight based on how similar A and B are at that point. Where they already agree, it keeps A. Where they diverge, it incorporates B. The Shift parameter adjusts how conservative (positive) or aggressive (negative) the blending is. No alpha needed — the math decides.
workshop.method.dare.desc: Drop And REscale — randomly drops most of B's training changes and rescales the survivors to compensate. Neural networks are redundant, so even dropping 90% of changes often preserves the effect. Produces surprisingly clean results from messy finetunes.
workshop.method.dare_ties.desc: Combines DARE and TIES — randomly drops changes first, then trims the survivors by magnitude. The most aggressive filtering. Best when B is a very noisy finetune and you want only the absolute strongest signal.
workshop.method.della.desc: Like DARE but smarter about what it drops — drop probability is inversely proportional to magnitude, so large important changes survive while small noisy ones are more likely to be removed. Produces slightly more reliable results than DARE's uniform random masking.
workshop.method.della_ties.desc: Combines DELLA and TIES — magnitude-weighted dropout first, then trims survivors by magnitude. Like DARE-TIES but with smarter dropout that preferentially keeps important parameters.
workshop.method.slerp.desc: Spherical interpolation — preserves the magnitude of weight vectors instead of averaging them. Usually produces sharper, more vibrant results than Weighted Sum at the same alpha. Best for blending two models of similar quality.
workshop.method.star.desc: Spectral Truncation and Rescale — decomposes B's training via SVD and strips noisy components before merging. Produces cleaner results than element-wise methods, especially from overtrained or messy finetunes. The Eta parameter controls how aggressively noise is removed.
workshop.method.svd_blend.desc: Aligns both models' spectral decompositions via Procrustes rotation, then interpolates structure and magnitude together in spectral space. Smoother than Weighted Sum because it respects the geometric relationship between feature directions rather than averaging raw weights.
workshop.method.svd_struct_a_mag_b.desc: Decomposes both models via SVD, then takes A's feature directions (what the layer detects) and B's magnitudes (how strongly it responds). Example: photorealism model's composition + anime model's vibrancy. Produces results impossible from any weight-averaging method.
workshop.method.svd_struct_b_mag_a.desc: The inverse — takes B's feature directions (what the layer detects) and A's magnitudes (how strongly it responds). Same concept as Structure A + Mag B but swapped. Try both and compare — the results are surprisingly different.
workshop.method.ties.desc: Trim, Elect Sign & Merge — extracts B's training over A, then trims away the weakest changes, keeping only the most significant ones. The Density parameter controls how aggressively to trim. Great for noisy finetunes where you want only the strongest signal.
workshop.method.weighted_sum.desc: The simplest merge — blends every weight between A and B by the alpha value. Good starting point for any merge. If results look washed out, try SLERP instead.

showme.models.intro.text: Studio generates with the models in the folders you choose — there is no Load button. Let’s point it at yours. This walkthrough takes you to Settings and back.
showme.models.folders.text: Settings → General → Model folders. One folder per kind of file: Checkpoint, Text encoder, VAE, plus Auto Detail detectors, LoRAs, embeddings and upscalers. Type a path or press Browse… to open the folder window. Studio lists only the files directly inside each folder, not subfolders.
showme.models.save.text: Press Save folders. Every folder is checked together; if one can’t be used, nothing changes and your current folders keep working. A folder on another computer needs Allow network model folders switched on first.
showme.models.pick.text: Back on the Canvas, the Model box lists your checkpoints. Models that need them also use a Text encoder and a VAE — leave VAE on Automatic unless the model asks for one. Added a file later? Press the ↻ button beside the box.
showme.models.generate.text: Choosing a model does not load it. Generate loads what you chose, so the first image after a change takes longer.
showme.inpaint.area.text: The bar above the canvas has the inpaint settings. Only Masked redraws just the masked area at full detail, with Padding of surrounding context; Whole Picture redraws the full canvas. Fill chooses what is under the mask: Original keeps it, Fill starts from flat colour (best for removing things).
showme.softInpaint.soft.text: With the new mask selected, the bar above the canvas has Opacity and Hardness. Turn Hardness down and paint over the house: the edge fades out. The selected row says used for inpainting — that is the mask Generate sends.
showme.masks.intro.text: Besides the Inpaint mask, a picture can hold any number of named masks. They live in the Masks panel, inside Layers. The mask selected there is the one Generate inpaints with.
showme.masks.new.text: Click New mask. A mask appears in the list and the Inpaint Mask tool is picked. Paint over the house; − Subtract in the bar above the canvas erases. Double-click a name to rename it, the eye hides its overlay, the swatch changes its colour.
showme.masks.selection.text: Load as selection turns the selected mask into a selection (Shift adds, Alt subtracts, Shift+Alt intersects); Ctrl+click on a row does the same. The button beside it, Save selection as mask, goes the other way: draw a selection with any selection tool, then keep it as a mask.
showme.masks.range.text: From range… makes a soft mask from the picture itself: its highlights, midtones, shadows, or a colour range. Try Shadows — no painting needed. From word… does the same from a word of the prompt, for pictures Studio made with heatmap recording on (see the Codex).
showme.masks.use.text: The selected row says used for inpainting. Write a prompt and press Generate: only that mask changes. Masks are kept per tab, come back after a reload, and are saved as layer masks when you export a PSD.
showme.outpaint.intro.text: Outpaint makes the picture bigger and asks the model to paint the new space so it continues the scene. There is no button for it: it lives in the canvas right-click menu.
showme.outpaint.menu.text: Right-click the canvas and choose Outpaint…. (Canvas Size…, just above it, grows or trims the canvas without generating.)
showme.outpaint.dialog.text: Choose how far to extend each side, in pixels (rounded to a multiple of 8). Overlap is how much of the existing edge is repainted so the join is seamless. Refine new area adds a second, light pass for crisper detail — slower, and off unless you choose it. Press Extend.
showme.outpaint.generate.text: Studio fills the new area from the picture’s edge on a layer called Outpaint fill, masks it, and sets up inpainting. Describe what should appear, then press Generate (this needs a model). It takes about as long as one normal generation, even on large pictures.
showme.canvasMenu.intro.text: Right-click anywhere on the canvas. This menu has things that have no toolbar button — start by right-clicking the picture now.
showme.canvasMenu.selection.text: With a selection active (try the rectangle tool, M), the menu adds Invert, Feather, Grow and Shrink Selection…, Copy/Cut/Delete, and Smart Patch — which fills the selection from the picture around it, with no model.
showme.canvasMenu.layers.text: Below that: New Layer, Duplicate Layer, Merge Down, Flatten Visible, then Canvas Size… and Outpaint… (only here).
showme.canvasMenu.save.text: At the bottom: Open in New Tab opens the flattened picture as a PNG in a new browser tab (allow pop-ups for Studio), and Save as PNG, JPEG, WebP or a layered PSD.
showme.layers.adjust.text: The buttons above the list add adjustment layers — Brightness/Contrast, Hue/Saturation and Levels — that change everything beneath them without touching the pixels. Delete the layer to undo it. The Masks panel below the list is covered in its own Show Me.
showme.clone.modes.text: The tool has three modes: Clone copies exactly; Heal copies the source’s detail but keeps the colour and light of where you paint; Patch needs no source at all. There is a separate Show Me for Patch.
showme.smartPatch.intro.text: The pink square again. Patch removes small things like this from their surroundings — no source point, no model, no waiting.
showme.smartPatch.mode.text: Press K for the Clone tool, then click Patch in the bar above the canvas.
showme.smartPatch.paint.text: Paint over the pink square, covering it fully, then let go. On release it is filled from the picture around it. If the result isn’t right, undo (Ctrl+Z) and paint a slightly larger area.
showme.smartPatch.selection.text: Same thing with a selection: draw one around a blemish, right-click inside it and choose Smart Patch. It works best on small things against a plain-ish background. For anything large, mask it and use inpainting.
showme.paintMixer.intro.text: The brush can mix colours like wet paint: it picks up the colour under it and carries it along the stroke, so blue and yellow make green, not just yellow on top.
showme.paintMixer.on.text: Pick the brush (B) and switch Mix on in the bar above the canvas. Amount is how much of the picked-up colour the brush carries: 0 is the plain brush colour, 100 only what it picked up.
showme.paintMixer.paint.text: Paint a wide blue stroke. Change the foreground colour to yellow and paint across it. Where they meet you get green, and the colours smear into each other along the stroke. Turn Mix off to go back to ordinary painting.
showme.develop.intro.text: Develop adjusts the whole picture — or just part of it. For a part you need a mask. We made one for you: a mask of this picture’s shadows, in the Masks panel.
showme.develop.local.text: In the Develop tab, Local adjustments sits right under the global sliders. Press Add local adjustment and choose the mask. Then move Exposure, Contrast, Highlights, Shadows, Whites, Blacks, Temperature, Tint, Saturation or Vibrance: they change only what the mask covers.
showme.develop.ba.text: B/A flips between before and after, and Reset clears every Develop adjustment. The switch beside the title turns Develop on or off without losing your settings.
moduleTour.gallery.empty.text: This is the Gallery — a browser for your generated images. It shows the folders you link. Press Choose folder & scan to link your Studio results folder, or any folder of pictures; the sidebar, search and grid appear once it has images.
